entries.title: Anchoring Effect – when a starting number pulls later estimates toward it
entries.description:
Anchoring Effect is the tendency for an initial number or reference value to pull a later numerical judgment toward it, even when the starting point is weak or not very useful.

Where can it show up?
- Negotiation – the first price can influence the range of later offers.
- Forecasts and estimates – an early target, budget, deadline, or rough guess can shape later numbers before the evidence is fully reviewed.
- AI-assisted decisions – a suggested score or recommendation can become the starting point for a person’s later judgment.

A better check
- Make an independent estimate before seeing a suggested number when that is practical.
- Ask what evidence would justify moving far away from the starting value.
- Compare the estimate with base rates, completed cases, ranges, or independent estimates instead of adjusting only from the anchor.
- Do not assume every number creates the same effect. Random, incidental, or clearly irrelevant anchors can be weaker than meaningful starting points.
